group.title: Talking and writing
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A talk between two or more people.
examples: We had a long {conversation} about music.
wrong: They had a conversation without saying a word.

words.meaning: To call out very loudly.
examples: He {yelled} for help from the window.
wrong: She yelled so softly that nobody heard.

words.meaning: Your name written in your own special way.
examples: Please put your {signature} at the bottom of the form.
wrong: He typed someone else’s name as his signature.

words.meaning: The person who is making a phone call.
examples: The {caller} didn’t say her name.
wrong: The caller was the person who picked up the phone.

words.meaning: To say hello to someone when you meet them.
examples: She {greeted} us with a big smile.
wrong: He greeted me by walking past without a word.

words.meaning: When you tell people someone’s name the first time they meet.
examples: After the {introductions}, we all sat down.
wrong: The introduction happened after they knew each other for years.

words.meaning: To manage to speak to someone on the phone.
examples: I called three times but couldn’t {get through}.
wrong: I got through to her, so we never spoke.

words.meaning: A machine that records messages when nobody answers the phone.
examples: I left a message on her {answering machine}.
wrong: The answering machine answers your questions about math.

words.meaning: To phone someone.
examples: I’ll {call up} Grandma tonight.
wrong: I called up my friend by writing him a letter.

words.meaning: To get something that someone sent you.
examples: Did you {receive} my email?
wrong: I received the letter, but it never came.

words.meaning: The numbers you dial to call someone.
examples: Can I have your {phone number}?
wrong: I wrote his phone number on the map to find his house.

words.meaning: A phone you carry with you that works without wires.
examples: I left my {cellphone} at home.
wrong: My cellphone is fixed to the wall in the kitchen.

words.meaning: To wait on the phone without hanging up.
examples: Please {hold the line} while I find the manager.
wrong: She asked me to hold the line, so I hung up.

words.meaning: A word used before a name at the start of a letter or email.
examples: {Dear} Mr. Brown, thank you for your letter.
wrong: I ended my email with dear and then signed my name.

words.meaning: Friendly words used to end a letter or card.
examples: {Best wishes}, Sarah.
wrong: She started her angry letter of complaint with best wishes.

words.meaning: A polite word to end a formal letter, before your name.
examples: Yours {sincerely}, John Smith.
wrong: I wrote sincerely at the very start of the letter.

words.meaning: Letters and packages sent by plane.
examples: I sent the letter by {airmail} so it arrives fast.
wrong: Airmail is carried slowly by boat.

words.meaning: To answer someone’s phone message with your own message.
examples: I’ll {text back} when I finish work.
wrong: She texted back by not answering at all.

words.meaning: A message that helps you not forget something.
examples: I set a {reminder} for the dentist.
wrong: The reminder made me forget the meeting.

words.meaning: When you ask for something politely.
examples: I sent a {request} for more information.
wrong: His request was an order he did not want anything.

words.meaning: A machine you use to talk to someone far away.
examples: The {telephone} in the office rang all day.
wrong: I watched a movie on the telephone in the hallway.

words.meaning: A small mistake made when typing.
examples: There’s a {typo} in your email: ’teh’ should be ’the’.
wrong: A typo is a word that is spelled perfectly.

words.meaning: A phone number you call by mistake.
examples: Sorry, you have the {wrong number}.
wrong: I called the wrong number and spoke to the person I wanted.

words.meaning: A polite way to ask someone to say something again.
examples: ’{Pardon}? I didn’t hear you.’
wrong: He said pardon because he heard every word clearly.

words.meaning: To hold someone’s hand and move it up and down when you meet.
examples: They {shook hands} and said hello.
wrong: They shook hands without touching.

words.meaning: To answer a letter or message.
examples: She never {wrote back} to my email.
wrong: He wrote back before he read my letter.

words.meaning: To reply to someone later.
examples: I’ll {get back to} you tomorrow with an answer.
wrong: I’ll get back to you never, so wait for my call.

words.meaning: A list of the names, numbers and addresses of people you know.
examples: I added her email to my {address book}.
wrong: An address book is a novel about houses.

words.meaning: A first version of a letter or message that is not finished.
examples: I saved a {draft} of the email to send later.
wrong: The draft was the final copy, already sent.

words.meaning: The sound you make when you speak or sing.
examples: I knew it was her from her {voice} on the phone.
wrong: She heard his voice in the photo.

words.meaning: To greet someone, or to send them a friendly hello.
examples: {Say hi} to your parents for me!
wrong: He said hi to me as he left forever.

words.meaning: A phone setting so everyone in the room can hear the call.
examples: Put the call on {speakerphone} so we can all hear.
wrong: I used speakerphone so only I could hear the call.

words.meaning: A phone at home or in an office that is connected by a wire.
examples: Call me on my {landline} at home.
wrong: I carry my landline in my pocket everywhere.

words.meaning: A person who answers calls and connects callers to the right person.
examples: The {operator} put me through to the sales team.
wrong: The operator never answers any calls.

words.meaning: A group of numbers in an address that helps mail arrive.
examples: Don’t forget the {zip code} on the envelope.
wrong: The zip code is the name of the person you write to.

words.meaning: The money you pay to send a letter or package.
examples: How much is the {postage} for this letter?
wrong: Postage is free food you get at the post office.

words.meaning: Friendly wishes, often at the end of an email.
examples: Kind {regards}, Tom.
wrong: She sent her regards to show she hated him.

words.meaning: To wait for a short time.
examples: {Hang on}, I’ll get a pen.
wrong: Hang on means please hurry and leave now.

words.meaning: To write down what a caller says for someone who is not there.
examples: She’s out. Can I {take a message}?
wrong: I took a message, but I wrote nothing down.

words.meaning: In a voice that others can hear.
examples: Please read the letter {aloud}.
wrong: She read aloud, so nobody could hear a word.
